There is no fault in any of you; only a little effort is needed: by bathing and giving at the Gautami and offering rice-balls,
brahmapuran:123:168	I am freed from the three brahmin-slayings and go to heaven. O daughter of Janaka, you have spoken as befits your family.
brahmapuran:123:169	Women of noble family carry one across to the far shore of the ocean of existence. By the grace of the Godavari, what here is hard to attain?
When they agreed and began, the slayer of foes could find no food to offer as the rice-ball; then he spoke to Lakshmana.
Lakshmana said humbly, "There are ingudi fruits, and their oil-cake," and brought it almost at once.
Then Rama, resolving to offer his father a rice-ball of oil-cake in the Ganga, became downcast and sorrowful.
A divine voice arose there: "Give up your sorrow, O prince. You have lost your kingdom and come to the forest; are you not without possessions?
You are honest and devoted to dharma; you should not grieve here. It is he who practises dharma while hiding his wealth who is the sinner.
It is heard in all the scriptures, O Rama, listen carefully: whatever food a man eats, O king, that same food is eaten by his gods."
When the rice-ball fell to the ground he did not then see his father; and the place where the corpse fell is the unsurpassed Shavatirtha,
whose very remembrance destroys the mass of great sins. There came the guardians of the worlds, the Rudras, the Adityas and the two Ashvins,
each mounted on his own celestial car; among them, on the finest car, exceedingly radiant and praised by the Kinnaras,
his father shone in their midst with a form like the sun. Not seeing his own father, but seeing the gods in their cars,
Rama, with joined palms, said, "Where is my father?" Then a divine voice spoke, addressing Rama and Sita:
King Dasharatha is freed from the three brahmin-slayings; see him, dear one, surrounded by the gods. And the gods too said to him:

You are blessed, you have done your duty, O Rama; your father has gone to heaven. He who lifts his forefathers out of the host of hells
brahmapuran:123:183	is blessed, and by that accomplished one the three worlds are adorned. See him, O mighty-armed one, freed from sin and radiant as the sun.
brahmapuran:123:184	Even with every kind of wealth, a sinner is like a burnt tree; even without possessions, a virtuous man shines like the moon-crested Shiva.
Seeing his son, the king spoke, greeting him with blessings:
You have done your duty; blessings on you. I have been delivered by you, O sinless one. Blessed in this world is the son who delivers his ancestors.
Then the hosts of gods, to accomplish the gods' purpose, said to Rama, best of men, "Go, dear one, as you please." Hearing their words, Rama said to the gods:
O gods, what duty remains for me toward my elder, my father?

No river equals the Ganga, no son is like you, no god is equal to Shiva, and no mantra equals the pranava.
brahmapuran:123:190	By you, O Rama, every duty to your elders has been fulfilled; your ancestors have been delivered by you, their son, O giver of honour. Let all go to their own abodes, and you too go as you please.
Delighted by the gods' words, Lakshmana's elder brother, with Sita, having seen the greatness of the Ganga, spoke in wonder:
Ah, this power of the Ganga has no equal in the three worlds. We are blessed, for we have seen the Ganga, purifier of the three worlds.
Filled with great joy, he installed the god Maheshvara and carefully worshipped that Lord with the sixteen offerings,
worshipping the Lord of thirty-six kalas together with his attendant deities; then, with joined palms, Rama praised Shankara:

I bow to Shambhu, the ancient Person; I bow to the all-knowing one of boundless being; I bow to Rudra, the imperishable Lord; I bow to Sharva, I bow with my head.
brahmapuran:123:196	I bow to the supreme, imperishable God; I bow to Uma's lord, teacher of the worlds; I bow to him who tears away poverty; I bow to the remover of disease.
brahmapuran:123:197	I bow to the auspicious one of inconceivable form; I bow to him who is the seed of the universe's origin; I bow to the cause of its preservation; I bow to its destroyer.
brahmapuran:123:198	I bow to the imperishable beloved of Gauri; I bow to him who is ever the perishable and the imperishable; I bow to him whose form is consciousness and whose being is immeasurable; I bow with my head to the three-eyed one.
brahmapuran:123:199	I bow always to him who is compassionate to beings, and also terrifying; I bow to the giver of all that is desired; I bow first to Someshvara, lord of Uma.
brahmapuran:123:200	I bow to him whose eyes are the three Vedas; I bow to him who is beyond the three forms; I bow to the holy one beyond being and non-being; I bow to the remover of sin.
brahmapuran:123:201	I bow to him devoted to the welfare of the universe, who bears many forms; he who is the protector of the universe and the director of being and non-being — I bow to that Lord of the universe.
brahmapuran:123:202	The lord of sacrifice, who is now the offering to gods and ancestors, the goal of the worlds, the eternal Shiva who when worshipped gives everything — I bow to that chosen deity who delights in giving.
brahmapuran:123:203	I bow to Someshvara, who is bound to his devotees; I bow to that lord of Uma, the victorious; I bow with my head to the lord of Vighneshvara and Nandi, who loves his sons.
brahmapuran:123:204	I bow to the god who destroys the grief and sorrow of worldly existence; I bow to the bearer of the moon; I bow to the praiseworthy Lord who holds the Ganga; I bow to Uma's consort, best of gods.
brahmapuran:123:205	I bow to him whose lotus feet are worshipped by gods and demons led by Brahma, Vishnu and Indra; I bow to him who wished for three eyes to behold the Goddess's face.
brahmapuran:123:206	Worshipped with the five nectars, perfume, fine incense and lamps, with various flowers and many mantras, with kinds of food and every offering — to that Lord with Uma I bow.
Then the blessed Shambhu said to Rama and Lakshmana, "Choose boons; blessings on you." Rama said to the bull-bannered god:

O best of gods, may every undertaking of those who devotedly please you with this hymn succeed, O Maheshvara.
brahmapuran:123:209	And those whose ancestors, O Shambhu, have fallen into the ocean of hell — purified by the offering of rice-balls and the like here, may they go to heaven.
brahmapuran:123:210	Sins committed since birth, and wrongs of mind, speech and body — may they be destroyed at once merely by bathing here.
brahmapuran:123:211	Whatever those who give here with devotion to supplicants, even a trifle, O Shambhu, may all of it be imperishable and bear fruit for the givers.
So be it, said Shankara to Rama, delighted. When that best of gods had gone, Rama too, with his followers,
slowly went to the region where the Gautami arose. From then on that tirtha has been called Ramatirtha.
An arrow fell there from the hand of the compassionate Lakshmana; that became Banatirtha, which wards off all calamities.
Where Saumitri bathed and worshipped Shankara, that tirtha became Lakshmanatirtha, and likewise Sitatirtha,
able to uproot the whole mass of sins of every kind. He by contact with whose feet the Ganga became the purifier of the three worlds —
where he bathed, what can be said of its excellence? No tirtha anywhere is like that Ramatirtha.
Whatever the king of the gods attempted against the being in the womb, the energy of the sage Kashyapa was unfailing and hard to overcome.
Then thousand-eyed Purandara took up his thunderbolt and, wishing to enter within, waited there a long time.
Seeing her asleep at twilight with her head to the north, the wielder of the thunderbolt said, "This is the opening," and entered Diti's womb.
The being within, seeing Indra with weapon raised and bent on killing it, spoke again and again without fear:

Why do you not protect me, O wielder of the thunderbolt? You wish to kill your brother. Outside battle there is no greater sin than killing.
brahmapuran:124:59	Only in battle, O mighty-armed Shakra — fight me when I have come out. This is not fitting for you.
brahmapuran:124:60	You are Shatakratu, the thousand-eyed, husband of Shachi, Purandara, thunderbolt in hand, king of the gods; this does not befit you, O lord.
brahmapuran:124:61	Or if you wish to fight, act so that I may come out, O mighty-armed one; step aside from this path.
brahmapuran:124:62	The great do not take a wrong path even in distress. I am unlearned, unarmed, and have no store of weapons;
brahmapuran:124:63	you are learned, O wielder of the thunderbolt — are you not ashamed to kill me? The nobly born never do a blameworthy deed.
brahmapuran:124:64	What would come of killing me — fame, or merit? Brothers in the womb are killed out of desire — what manliness is that?
brahmapuran:124:65	Or if you truly have a craving to fight me, brother... Then he stood ready before the thunderbolt-wielder with his fist raised.

The slayer of a child, the slayer of a brahmin, and the betrayer of trust — such is the fruit, Shakra; why are you set on killing me?
brahmapuran:124:67	He at whose command this whole world, moving and unmoving, goes on — if he kills me, a child, what fame is that, what manliness?
As it spoke thus, he cut the embryo with his thunderbolt. Those blinded by anger and greed have no pity anywhere.
It did not die; then in pain they said, "We are your brothers." Again he cut the pieces, and they cried, "Do not kill us!"
Your own trusting brothers in their mother's womb, O Shatakratu! In minds whose judgment hatred has destroyed there is not a particle of compassion.
Each piece so cut was alive, with hands, feet and the rest; seeing them unharmed, seven times seven, he was greatly astonished.
Many beautiful forms, as if one, lay in the womb; the many forms wept, and Hari said, "Do not weep."
Thus they became the Maruts, strong and of great vigour. Still in the womb, their confusion gone, they spoke to one another and to Shakra,
and called on Agastya, tiger among sages, in whose hermitage their mother was staying: "Our father is like a brother to you and greatly values your friendship.
We know your mind is affectionate toward us, O sage. The thunderbolt-wielder has set about what not even an outcaste would do."
Hearing these words, Agastya went in haste and comforted Diti, who was in anguish from the pain of her womb.
There Agastya, greatly enraged, cursed the lord of Shachi:
In battle, O Hari, may your enemies always see your back. For the proud this alone is death while still alive: that foes in battle see their backs as they flee.
Diti too, in anger, cursed Indra while he was still inside her womb:
You have not acted with manliness, so this shall be your curse: humiliated by women, you will fall from your kingdom, O Hari.
Meanwhile Kashyapa the Prajapati came there, distressed, having heard from Agastya what Shakra had done. Shakra, inside the womb, spoke fearfully to his father:
I fear Agastya and Diti, and dare not step outside.
Meanwhile Kashyapa the Prajapati, arriving and seeing his son's deed and that he was still within the womb, and hearing the curses of Diti and Agastya, was grieved.
Come out, Shakra, my son. What sin is this you have done? Those born of a pure family do not set their minds on sin.
The thunderbolt-wielder came out, ashamed, with face cast down, and said, "A man's very bearing declares whether his conduct is good or bad.
Whatever is declared best here, that I will certainly do."
Then Kashyapa came to me with the guardians of the worlds, told the whole story, and with the gods asked me again
about the pacifying of Diti's embryo, the thousand-eyed one's release from the curse, and friendship between all those in the womb and Indra,
their good health, the blamelessness of Shachi's husband, and in due course the undoing of the curse given by Agastya.
Then I spoke courteously to Kashyapa: "O Prajapati Kashyapa, with the Vasus and the guardians of the worlds,
and with Indra, go quickly to the Gautami, O giver of honour. Bathe there and, with all of them, praise Mahesha.
Then by Shiva's grace all will be well." Saying "So be it," Kashyapa went to the Gautami.
Having bathed, he praised the Lord of gods with these very words: "Two alone are proclaimed to remove all sorrow — the holy river Gautami, or Shiva, the mine of compassion.
Protect us, O Shankara, lord of gods; protect us, you who are saluted by the worlds; protect us, O purifier, lord of speech; protect us, you who are adorned with serpents.
Protect us, O Dharma, rider of the bull; protect us, you whose eyes are the three Vedas; protect us, O bearer of the earth, lord of Lakshmi; protect us, O Sharva, clad in elephant hide.
Protect us, O lord, slayer of Tripura; protect us, you who are adorned with the half-moon; protect us, O lord of sacrifice, Someshvara; protect us, O giver of what is desired.
Protect us, O abode of compassion; protect us, O giver of blessings; protect us, O origin of all; protect us, O protector, O Vasava.
Protect us, O Sun, lord of wealth; protect us, you who are saluted by Brahma; protect us, O lord of the universe, lord of the Siddhas; protect us, O perfect one; salutations to you.
For embodied beings whose minds are troubled by wandering in the dreadful wilderness of worldly existence, you alone are the refuge, O Shiva, ocean of compassion."
As he praised thus, the bull-bannered god appeared before him and offered a boon to Kashyapa the Prajapati.
Kashyapa humbly spoke to Shiva and described at length what Indra had done:
the curse, the harm to the sons, their mutual enmity, Shakra's incurring of sin, and his being cursed as well. Then Vrishakapi spoke to Diti and to Agastya:

Your sons, the Maruts, forty-nine in number, shall all be fortunate and shall have a share in sacrifices.
brahmapuran:124:104	They shall always live joyfully together with Indra.
brahmapuran:124:105	Wherever Indra has a share of oblation in a sacrifice, there the Maruts shall be first; of this there is no doubt.
brahmapuran:124:106	None shall ever conquer Shakra when he is with the Maruts; he shall always be victorious. Dwell in happiness, O Prajapati.
brahmapuran:124:107	From today, those who wrongfully kill their brothers shall always suffer the ruin of their line and misfortune.
Shambhu also spoke earnestly to Agastya, tiger among sages:
Do not be angry with Shachi's husband, O sage. Be at peace, O wise one; the Maruts have become immortal.
Shiva, the bull-bannered god, graciously spoke to Diti as well:

Thinking, 'May I have one son adorned with lordship over the three worlds,' you devoted yourself to austerity.
brahmapuran:124:112	Today that has borne fruit for you: your sons are many-virtued and auspicious, strong and heroic, so cast off the pain in your heart. Ask for other boons too, fair-browed one, without fear.
Hearing these words of the God of gods, Diti bowed to Shambhu with joined palms and said:

The highest thing in the world is for parents to see a son, and it is especially dear to the mother, O you who are worshipped by the gods.
brahmapuran:124:115	Even a single son endowed with beauty, fortune, valour and prowess is prized — how much more when there are many!
brahmapuran:124:116	By your power my sons are surely strong and victorious; truly they are Indra's brothers and the sons of the Prajapati.
brahmapuran:124:117	By Agastya's grace and the Ganga's grace — where your grace is, O God, all is auspicious; what doubt is there?
brahmapuran:124:118	I am fulfilled; still, I devotedly make a request of you. Hear my words, O God, and do what is good for the world.
Told "Speak" by the Upholder of the world, Diti humbly said this:

Obtaining offspring is hard in this world, O you whom the gods revere; a son is especially dear to a mother — what more need be said?
brahmapuran:124:121	And if he is born virtuous, prosperous and long-lived, what use is heaven, O Lord of gods, or even the highest state?
brahmapuran:124:122	For all beings seeking reward here and hereafter, a virtuous son is always the thing desired. So grant this favour through bathing here.
brahmapuran:124:123	Childlessness is the fruit of great sin; if barrenness arises in a woman or a man,
brahmapuran:124:124	may that fault be destroyed merely by bathing here. Whoever bathes there, gives fruit, and recites this hymn
brahmapuran:124:125	shall obtain a son through three months of bathing and giving. A childless woman who bathes here shall obtain a son.
brahmapuran:124:126	Any woman who bathes there after her monthly bath shall obtain sons; and a pregnant woman who, within three months, devotedly here
brahmapuran:124:127	bathes with fruits, sees me, and praises me with this hymn shall bear a son equal to Shakra; there is no doubt.

Listen, Diti: for those who do not obtain a son because of the faults of their ancestors or the sin of stealing wealth, this is the supreme expiation there:
brahmapuran:124:129	by offering rice-balls there, pleasing the ancestors, and giving a little gold, a son will surely be born.
brahmapuran:124:130	The line of those who steal deposits and the like, who conceal jewels, and who neglect the shraddha rites does not grow.
brahmapuran:124:131	This shall be the way for the departed who were at fault; and for the living, may praiseworthy offspring be born through resorting to the tirtha.
brahmapuran:124:132	At the confluence of Diti's river and the Ganga, having bathed, the lord Siddheshvara — beginningless, endless, unageing, whose form is consciousness and eternal bliss,
brahmapuran:124:133	served by gods, sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas and lords of yoga, the great god in the form of the linga, full of light and free from all ill —
brahmapuran:124:134	whoever, keeping his vows, worships him daily with devotion and offerings, and praises him with this hymn on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days,
brahmapuran:124:135	and gives gold according to his means and feeds brahmins here at the Ganga, shall obtain a hundred sons.
brahmapuran:124:136	Having obtained all his desires, at the end he goes to Shiva's city. Whoever praises me anywhere with this hymn obtains a son within six months, even if barren, without doubt.
From then on that tirtha has been called Putratirtha; by bathing, giving and the like there one obtains all desires.
Because of the friendship with the Maruts it is called Mitratirtha; because of Indra's freedom from sin it is called Shakratirtha.
The tirtha where he regained Indra's glory is called Kamala. All these tirthas grant every wish.
Saying, "All this will come to pass," Shiva vanished, and they all, their purpose accomplished, went back as they had come. One hundred thousand merit-giving tirthas are proclaimed there.

He becomes prosperous, wise and heroic, flourishing with sons and grandsons. By offering rice-balls and the like there the ancestors attain liberation, and by bathing a man is freed from sin born of mind, speech and body.
After Yama's words, the Bearer of oblations likewise spoke to the two birds:

Those who, keeping their vows, recite my hymn on the southern bank — to them I give health, lordship, prosperity and beauty.
brahmapuran:125:52	Whoever recites this hymn anywhere has no fear of fire, even if it is only kept written in his house.
brahmapuran:125:53	The pure man who bathes and gives at Agnitirtha surely gains the fruit of the Agnishtoma sacrifice; there is no doubt.
From then on the wise know that tirtha as Yamya and Agneya, and also as Kapota and Uluka, called Hetyuluka.
There are three thousand tirthas there, as many hundreds, and ninety more, each a vessel of liberation.
By bathing and giving at them even men who have become ghosts are purified and, rich in sons and wealth, ascend to the auspicious heaven.
Tell us whether fire or water is the elder; you are the lord of the three worlds.
I said to all the sages who had come, keeping their vows: "Both are most worthy of worship in the world; from both the world is born.
From both come offerings to the gods and ancestors, and nectar too; from both come life in the world and the sustaining of the body.
There is no difference between them, so their seniority is held to be equal." So by my word neither of the two was the elder.
The best of sages held that one of the two must be the elder; not satisfied with my words, the ascetics went to Vayu:
Whose is the seniority? You are the life-breath, O Vayu; truth rests in you.
Vayu said, "Fire is the elder; everything is established in fire." Saying "No" to one another, the sages then went to the Earth:
O Earth, tell truly which is the elder; you are the support of all that moves and does not move.
The Earth too humbly said this to the sages who had come:
The eternal divine Waters are my own support; from the waters everything is born, and seniority rests in the waters.
Saying "No" to one another, the sages went to him who lies on the ocean of milk and praised the bearer of conch, discus and mace with various hymns:

He who knows the whole world, what will be and what is being born, hidden in the cave of the heart; the three worlds of wondrous varied form, all of which enter into him at the end;
brahmapuran:126:25	that which is imperishable, eternal and immeasurable, which the sages call knowable through the Vedas, resorting to which men gain what they desire — to that Reality, the Truth, we go for refuge.
brahmapuran:126:26	The yogis cannot find Vishnu's form, which is the elements, the great elements and the chief principle of the world. These sages have come here to ask; speak the truth here, O abode of the universe.
brahmapuran:126:27	You are the inner Self of all embodied beings; you alone are everything, and everything is in you, O Lord. Yet, alas, no one anywhere knows you, because of the power of Prakriti.
Then a bodiless divine voice, the Upholder of the world, said:
Worship both with austerity, devotion and discipline; whichever grants perfection first, that element is called the elder.
Saying "So be it," all the sages revered by the world went away, weary and dejected at heart, resorting to supreme detachment.
All of them, keeping their vows, went to the Gautami, sole mother of all worlds and purifier of the three worlds, to perform austerities.
They then set about worshipping the deity of the waters and Fire. To those who worshipped Fire and those who worshipped the Waters, the divine voice spoke there — Sarasvati, mother of the Vedas:

The Waters are the source of Fire, and purity is gained through water. How can those who worship Fire worship without water?
brahmapuran:126:34	Through the waters one becomes entitled to rites everywhere; until then a man is unfit for rites, impure and soiled,
brahmapuran:126:35	so long as that knower of the Veda has not plunged with faith into the cool waters. Therefore the Waters are the foremost, since they are remembered as mothers; seniority belongs to the Waters, who are above all the mothers of Fire.
The sages who expound the Veda heard these words and then concluded that seniority belongs to the Waters.
The tirtha where this took place at the sages' sacrificial session, O Narada, is called Tapastirtha and also Sattratirtha.
It is also called Agnitirtha, and known as Sarasvata; bathing and giving at them is auspicious and grants all desires.
There are fourteen hundred merit-giving tirthas here; bathing and giving at them grants heaven and liberation.
Where the sages' doubt was removed by her speech, Sarasvati became a river there, joined with the Ganga. What man could describe the greatness of that confluence?
Then all the priests went from the sacrifice to their own places. The son of the king's priest was known as Devapi.
The boy, seeing his mother but not his father, was bewildered and became deeply grieved.
He asked his mother, "Where has my father gone, mother? Without my father I cannot live; tell me the truth, mother.
Fie, fie on the life of the sinful who have no father! If you do not tell me, mother, I will enter water or fire."
His mother, the wife of the king's priest, said to her son, "Your father has been carried off to the netherworld by a demon, together with the king."
Where was he taken, by whom, how, and during what rite? Who looked on? Tell me where the demon dwells.
The demon Mithu carried off the king, consecrated in the sacrificial hall, with his wife and his priest, to Rasatala, while the hosts of gods looked on, in the presence of the fire and the brahmins.
Hearing his mother's words, Devapi considered what to do: "I shall look to the gods, or to Fire, or to the priests, or to the demons;
my father must be sought among these and nowhere else; that is my view." Having so decided, Devapi spoke to Bhara, the king's son:

By austerity, celibacy, vows and discipline I must bring back all who were taken to Rasatala.
brahmapuran:127:19	When a terrible defeat has occurred, what use is that vilest of men who does not strike back, whether he lives or dies?
brahmapuran:127:20	Rule the whole earth as your father Arshtishena did. Protect my mother, O king, until I return with my task accomplished; give me leave, Bhara.
Bhara, having carefully considered everything, said to Devapi:
Accomplish your aim and go happily; do not entertain the least worry.
Then Devapi, intent on meditating on the feet of the king of the immortals, diligently sought out the priests and bowed to each of them; and the boy Devapi, with joined palms, said:

You were to protect the sacrifice and the consecrated sacrificer, and the priest likewise, and the consecrated one's wife.
brahmapuran:127:25	While you looked on, the demon king destroyed the sacrifice and carried off the king and the others; that was not at all proper.
brahmapuran:127:26	Still, I think you ought to give them all back unharmed; otherwise you deserve a curse.

In a sacrifice Fire is worshipped first; Fire alone is the deity here. So we do not know; we are only servants of the fires.
brahmapuran:127:28	He, the bearer of oblations, is the giver and the enjoyer, the taker and the doer.
Leaving the priests behind, Devapi duly worshipped Jatavedas and laid the matter before Fire.

As the priests are, so am I — a servant of the gods. I carry the offerings to the gods; they are the enjoyers and the protectors.
brahmapuran:127:31	Summoning the gods carefully, I give each his share of the oblation; this is no fault of mine. So go to the gods.
Devapi went to the gods, bowed to each of them, and reported the priests' words, Fire's words, and his threat of a curse.

Summoned by Vedic mantras and by the priests in due order, we enjoy our shares of the oblation; we are not independent, O best of brahmins.
brahmapuran:127:34	So we always follow the Vedas and are directed by the Veda; we are dependent. Therefore, O brahmin, put this to the Vedas.
Devapi purified himself and carefully invoked the Vedas; through his meditation and austerity the Vedas appeared before him.
Bowing to the Vedas again and again, Devapi told them the words of the priests, of Fire, and of the gods.

We are dependent, dear one, subject to the will of the Lord — the support of the whole world, himself unsupported and stainless,
brahmapuran:127:38	the sole abode of all powers, the treasury of all riches. That Mahadeva is the creator, and that Maheshvara is the destroyer.
brahmapuran:127:39	We are made of sound, O brahmin; we speak and we know. This is our function: we will tell you what you ask.
brahmapuran:127:40	Who carried them off, his name, his city and his strength; that they have not been devoured or destroyed — this we know.
brahmapuran:127:41	We also know your capacity, and whom you must worship and where, so that you will have them before you again.
Hearing this and reflecting long in his heart, he said to the Vedas:
Let the Vedas tell me all of this exactly as it is, and I will recover all who were taken to the netherworld; salutations to you.

Go to the Gautami, Devapi, and praise Maheshvara there; well pleased, the compassionate one will surely grant your wish.
brahmapuran:127:45	Praised, the god Shiva will truly be pleased, O wise one. King Arshtishena and his virtuous wife Jaya,
brahmapuran:127:46	and your father Upamanyu, remain unharmed in the netherworld. By Mahesha's boon you will slay the demon Mithu and gain fame and merit; this can be done, and nothing else.
At the Vedas' word the boy Devapi went to the Gautami; having bathed and completed his rites, the brahmin praised Maheshvara:

I am a child, O Lord of lords, and you are my teacher of teachers. I have no power to praise you; O Shambhu, salutations to you.
brahmapuran:127:49	The scriptures do not know you, nor the gods, nor the sages, nor Brahma, nor even Vishnu; whatever you are, that you are — salutations to you.
brahmapuran:127:50	Those who are helpless, wretched, poor and sick, and those in the world who are sinful — you protect them, O Maheshvara.
brahmapuran:127:51	The heaven-dwellers, worshipped with austerity, disciplines and mantras, give their worshippers the fruit that you have given them, O Lord of the worlds.
brahmapuran:127:52	That seekers and givers obtain whatever they desire is no wonder; you are the one who reverses fortunes.
brahmapuran:127:53	Those who are ignorant, who are sinful, who are sunk in the ocean of hell — at the word 'Shiva' you protect them, O Lord, teacher of the world.
As he praised thus, the three-eyed god appeared before him and said:
Name a boon, Devapi; enough of this dejection, child.
I wish to recover the king, the queen, and my father and teacher, O Lord of the world, and the death of my enemy.
Hearing Devapi's words, the Lord of all said, "So be it," and by Shankara's command everything came to pass for Devapi.
Then Shambhu, compassionate to Devapi, spoke again and sent Nandi with his trident, O Narada.
Nandi went to Rasatala, slew Mithu and the chief demons, brought back his father and the others, and handed them over to him.
Then the wise Arshtishena's horse-sacrifice took place there. Fire, the priests, the gods, the Vedas and the sages said:

Where Shambhu, God of gods and Lord of the world, fond of his devotees, appeared in person to Devapi, that became Devatirtha.
brahmapuran:127:62	This tirtha will destroy all sins, grant men every success and bestow merit; and your fame will be everlasting.
When the horse-sacrifice was complete, the gods gave them boons; having bathed in the Ganga, their aims fulfilled, they ascended to heaven.
From then on there have been fifteen thousand eight hundred tirthas there on both banks; bathing and giving at them is known to be most fruitful.
Through the fault of their mingling seed with each other, both of Agni's offspring were so: the son Suvarna, taking many forms, assumed the forms of the best of the gods
and continually visited the wives of Indra, Vayu, Kubera, Varuna and the great sages, taking on the form each one loved.
At times that son of the Seer went to faithful wives in the form of their husbands, and, generous-hearted, sported with them constantly, fulfilling desire.
Having done so he would go elsewhere. And Dharma's wife too, named Suvarna, daughter of Svaha, became wanton; whoever's mind she entered,
that same Suvarna, taking the form of his wife, enjoyed husbands — men, asuras, gods, sages, ancestors and others endowed with beauty, generosity, steadiness and depth.
Whichever god's wife he desired, she took her form and enjoyed him, drawing his mind to the fulfilment of desire with many and varied arts.
Seeing this conduct of Suvarna, the son of Agni, and likewise of Agni's daughter, all the gods and asuras in anger cursed Agni's son and daughter:

Since this adulterous behaviour has been committed, this sinful conduct by deceit, O Bearer of oblations, let your son be adulterous and go everywhere.
brahmapuran:128:37	Likewise, O Agni, let Suvarna not be devoted to one nor satisfied with one, but consort with many embodied beings of various despised kinds; this shall be your daughter's fault.
Hearing these words of the curse, Agni, greatly frightened, came to me and said, "Tell me the remedy for my children."
Then I said, "O Fire, go to the Gautami, O mighty-armed one, praise Shankara there, and make this known to the Lord of the world:
'Through Maheshvara's seed lodged in my body such offspring was born to me.' Then, O Fire,
report this curse of the gods to the God. To protect his own offspring, Shambhu will bring about their welfare.
Praise the God and the Goddess with devotion; Shiva will be pleased, and then you will obtain your wishes concerning your children."
Then at my word Agni went to the Ganga and, with self-restraint, praised Maheshvara with words and hymns consonant with the Veda:

The ordainer of the whole universe, whose form is the universe, stainless, the first creator and self-born — I bow to that Lord of the world.
brahmapuran:128:45	He who, becoming fire, destroys; who creates in the form of water; who protects in the form of the sun — I bow to that three-eyed one.
Then the blessed Shambhu, infinite and imperishable, well pleased, offered a boon to Pavaka, worshipped by the gods.
Humbly he said to Shiva, "Your seed dwells in me; from it was born a lovely son, Suvarna, famed in the world,
and likewise a daughter, Suvarna, from it, O Lord of the world. Through the mingling of their seed with each other, and from that fault, both of them
became offspring tainted by adultery, O Shiva. All the gods have cursed them; grant them relief, O Lord."
At Agni's words Shambhu spoke these auspicious words:

From my seed, through you, was born Suvarna of great valour; all prosperities are gathered in this Suvarna — gold.
brahmapuran:128:52	So they will be, no doubt; O Fire, hear my word: he will be the purifier of all three worlds.
brahmapuran:128:53	He alone will be nectar in the world, he the favourite of the gods, he both enjoyment and liberation, he the fee of the sacrifice.
brahmapuran:128:54	He will be the beauty of all things, the teacher even of teachers. Know seed to be most excellent, and the seed that comes from me is the highest.
brahmapuran:128:55	Since it was placed especially in you, what question can there be? Without it everything is lacking; with it all riches are complete.
brahmapuran:128:56	All men without gold are dead though living; a rich man is honoured even without virtues, but a virtuous man without wealth is not.
brahmapuran:128:57	Therefore nothing will be higher than gold. And this Suvarna too, though excellent, will be fickle.
brahmapuran:128:58	All that she looks upon, though lacking, will become full — she who is to be won in the three worlds by austerity, japa and oblations.
brahmapuran:128:59	Something of her power and excellence is told, O Agni: she who dwells everywhere will come and go as she wanders.
brahmapuran:128:60	Suvarna will be Kamala herself, and pure. From today, though your two children act as they please,
brahmapuran:128:61	still there has never been and never will be merit like theirs.
Having said this, Shambhu, Shiva himself, manifested there in the form of a linga, desiring the welfare of all the worlds.
Having received boons for his children, Agni was then content; and Suvarna, Agni's daughter, lived happily and righteously with her husband Dharma,
and Fire's son too lived happily as he wished. Meanwhile, O sage, Agni's daughter Svarna —
the demon lord Shardula, overpowering Dharma, carried off by deceit that abode of fortune, good luck and charm.
The world-famed Suvarna was taken by him to Rasatala. Agni's son-in-law Dharma and Agni, the bearer of oblations,
praised Vishnu, lord of the world, again and again, and together made their purpose known to the mighty one.
Then Hari cut off Shardula's head with his discus; the goddess Suvarna, most beautiful in the world, was brought back by Vishnu.
Vishnu showed her, Maheshvara's daughter and Agni's beloved, to Maheshvara, O Narada.
Mahesha too was delighted and embraced her again and again. The place where the shining discus that had severed Shardula was washed
is known as the famous Chakratirtha, and also as Shardula. Where Suvarna was brought by Vishnu into Shankara's presence,
that tirtha should be known as Shankara, as Vaishnava, and as Siddha. Where Agni and the eternal Dharma attained bliss,
where tears of joy fell from Agni, O best of sages, a river arose called Ananda, and also Nandini.
Its confluence with the Ganga is holy, and Shiva is there; at that very confluence Suvarna still dwells in person today —
she who is known as Dakshayani, Shiva and Agneyi; Ambika, support of the world, Shiva, Katyayani, the Queen,
ever granting her devotees' wishes, adorning both banks. Where Agni performed austerities, that tirtha is Tapovana.
Such are the tirthas on both banks, O sage; bathing and giving at them is auspicious and grants all desires.
On the northern bank there are fourteen thousand, and on the southern bank sixteen thousand.
Here and there are tirthas with their distinguishing marks and their separate names; I tell them to you in brief.
Whoever hears these, or recites or remembers them, becomes fulfilled in all his desires there.
Whoever knows this story and bathes and so on there always becomes prosperous, and especially righteous.
West of Abjaka is the tirtha called Shardula; it surpasses all the tirthas beginning with Varanasi.
One who bathes there and salutes and offers libations to the ancestors and gods is freed from all sins and honoured in Vishnu's world.
Between Tapovana and Shardula lie countless tirthas; the greatness of each one of them cannot be described here by anyone.
Where Hanuman's foster mother, merely by plunging in, was freed from the form of a cat by the grace of Vishnu and the Ganga —
that tirtha I described to you earlier as Marjara; it is also called Hanumata, and its story was told before.
Now listen attentively to the story of Vrishakapa and Abjaka. There was one known as Hiranya, a mighty forefather of the Daityas.
Having performed austerities, he became very fierce and invincible to all the gods. His son too was mighty and ever hard for the gods to conquer,
famed as Mahashani; his wife was Parajita. Indra fought a war with him continuously for a long time.
Mahashani of great valour, ever at the forefront of battle, conquered Shakra along with his elephant and presented him to his father.
Having bound him together with his elephant, and then seeing that sister of his, the Daitya set aside his cruelty and handed him over to Hiranya.
The Daitya Hiranya, Mahashani's father, more ancient than the ancients, placed Shachi's husband in the netherworld and kept him under guard.
Having conquered Hari, Mahashani went to conquer Varuna; but Varuna, of great wisdom, gave his daughter to Mahashani.
Varuna also gave the ocean, his own abode, to Mahashani, and friendship arose between Varuna and Mahashani.
Varuni, Varuna's daughter, became dear to Mahashani. In valour, fame, heroism and strength
the great Daitya Mahashani had no equal in the three worlds. When the world was left without an Indra, all the gods took counsel:
Vishnu alone can give us an Indra; he alone is the slayer of Daityas. He is the seer of counsel; he will make another Indra.
Having taken counsel thus, the gods laid their plan before Vishnu; he said, "The great Daitya Mahashani cannot be slain by me."
